summary.title: Maslow's pyramid of code review
summary.one_liner: A framework that orders code review concerns into layers, from correctness at the base up to altruism at the top, where each layer depends on the one below it.
keywords: what to look for in code review
takeaways: Code review concerns can be ranked in layers: correct, secure, readable, elegant, altruist.
Each layer depends on the previous one; readability does not matter if the code charges the wrong customer.
Correctness questions cover edge cases, tests that survive later changes, and performance for the use case.
Security questions cover vulnerabilities, safe data storage, PII handling, denial-of-service risk, and input validation.
Small refactors and cleaning up unused code are favored over large refactors, which the author dropped after reader feedback.
summary.summary: This short essay by Charles-Axel Dein applies Maslow's hierarchy of needs to code review. It lists five layers, each with a set of guiding questions: correct, secure, readable, elegant, and altruist. The author argues that each layer requires the one below it, so a reviewer should first check that code works before judging its style. A February 18 update notes that the author removed the idea of large refactors in favor of small ones after Reddit discussion, and added a note on why layering matters.
